figures.caption: Figure 3: Targeted ablation vs. random layer removal for both models. Baseline performance (blue) collapses to similar levels under both targeted (red) and random (gray, with error bars) ablation, confirming that the magnitude of accuracy degradation depends primarily on the number of removed layers rather than their functional identity.

Figure 6: Correlation between Experiment 2 layer-wise metrics (x-axis: norm change or logit-lens KL divergence) and Experiment 1 accuracy drop (y-axis). For Qwen, norm change shows a significant positive correlation (r=0.35, p=0.006), confirming that layers transforming representations more also cause greater degradation when ablated. For Falcon, the relationship is weaker and inverted (r=−0.27, p=0.025), suggesting tighter functional integration where importance is not predicted by output magnitude alone. Logit-lens KL shows no significant correlation in either model.

Figure 1: Radar chart showing benchmark performance under baseline and group ablation conditions. Both models show severe degradation when either component is removed, with distinctive per-benchmark profiles. The near-collapse on GSM8K (→0) under all conditions is clearly visible, while HellaSwag shows the most asymmetric response.

Table 1: Group ablation results across five benchmarks. Values show absolute score; parentheses show change from baseline (∆). Conditions marked with ∗ indicate that the mean score drop across all benchmarks has a bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero. Note that individual benchmarks may vary: TruthfulQA shows non-significant drops under some conditions.

Table 6: Falcon-H1 positional ablation: removing all components of one type within a positional third. Early-layer ablation causes substantially more damage than late-layer ablation for both SSM and attention.

Table 2: WikiText-2 perplexity under group ablation. The alternative component (linear attention for Qwen, SSM for Falcon) causes far greater perplexity degradation than attention, revealing its role as the language modeling backbone.

Figure 4: Mean accuracy drop (across MMLU and ARC-Challenge) when ablating a single layer’s component. Early layers show 2–5× larger drops than late layers, with the first layer being especially critical. The SSM gradient in Falcon is steeper than the attention gradient.

Figure 5: Layer-wise ablation impact (∆ accuracy from baseline) for both models, disaggregated by benchmark. Warm colors indicate larger degradation. The top-left concentration confirms that early-layer ablations cause the most damage across both architectures and all benchmarks.

Figure 2: WikiText-2 perplexity under group ablation (log scale). The order-of-magnitude difference between removing the alternative component vs. attention reveals the asymmetric backbone role: linear attention (Qwen) and SSM (Falcon) are the primary language modeling engines.

Figure 7: Score drop heatmap (Experiment 3) across all model–condition–benchmark combinations. Warm colors indicate larger degradation. GSM8K consistently shows the largest drops (top row region), while TruthfulQA is the most resilient (near-zero or negative drops). The cross-architecture consistency of these patterns suggests that task-dependent component reliance is a general property of hybrid models.
